item.title: Morning Brief — Morning Brief for Saturday, May 23, 2026
item.description: Senate Republicans recoil from Trump's anti-weaponization fund and stall a major immigration package, House leaders delay an Iran war powers vote they looked in danger of losing, the Export-Import Bank launches ExportAI to push American artificial intelligence abroad, Nvidia's blockbuster quarter keeps the AI boom alive while raising the standard again, Columbus uses the Sawyer Towers demolition to press tougher landlord accountability, Columbus City Schools enters the implementation phase after
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Saturday, May 23rd, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

COHOST: This morning feels like a reality check. A lot of institutions are still moving, but several of the biggest stories are about hesitation, delay, and what happens when leaders discover they do not have as much control as they thought.

HOST: We start in Washington, where the sharpest political development in the last twenty-four hours is the Senate Republican revolt that blew up a major immigration enforcement package. Associated Press reports Republicans pushed back hard enough against President Trump that leadership shelved the roughly seventy billion dollar bill rather than force a vote they could not confidently win.

HOST: The immediate problem was not the core border and deportation money. The problem was that the bill picked up two Trump priorities that many Republicans did not want to defend: roughly one point eight billion dollars for what the administration called an anti-weaponization fund, plus another billion dollars tied to security and construction around a planned White House ballroom. What had been sold as a clean enforcement package turned into a loyalty test, and Senate Republicans blinked.

COHOST: That is the part that matters this morning. Yesterday this looked like a messaging headache. Today it looks more like a governing limit.

HOST: Exactly. The continuity here matters because the story advanced. This is no longer just an embarrassing add-on or a bad headline. It is now evidence that even on immigration, one of the president's strongest issues, congressional Republicans can still get tangled up by the president's own demands. If leadership comes back in early June with a stripped-down version, that will tell you they heard the warning. If they cannot, then the bigger takeaway is that internal GOP resistance is becoming more operational and less symbolic.

HOST: The second national story is another delay, but on a much more serious question. AP reports House Republican leaders called off a vote on legislation that would force President Trump to withdraw from the war with Iran after it became clear they might not have the votes to kill it. So instead of beating the resolution, leadership postponed the confrontation into June.

COHOST: Which means Congress is not exactly ending the war, but it is also no longer pretending the politics are simple.

HOST: Right. That is why this remains an active story. The fresh development is the delay itself, because delays in Congress are often a proxy for uncertainty in the vote count. The White House can still argue that hostilities have effectively ended or changed form, but lawmakers in both parties are clearly not done testing that claim. And every sign that more Republicans are uneasy about the war matters outside Washington too, because this still runs straight through oil, inflation pressure, shipping, consumer confidence, and interest rates.

HOST: If you are trying to read the next few days clearly, watch whether the administration offers a more concrete definition of success in Iran, and whether skeptical lawmakers keep pressing for an actual vote rather than another procedural timeout.

HOST: On the AI and technology front, the clearest government move is now official. The Export-Import Bank announced Thursday that it is launching ExportAI, an initiative designed to speed financing for American artificial intelligence exports and expand the global reach of U.S. AI systems. In plain language, Washington wants foreign buyers to find it easier to purchase the American AI stack, with the United States using export finance more aggressively as part of the technology competition.

COHOST: So this is not just about regulating AI at home. It is about selling it abroad before rivals do.

HOST: That is the key point. We have talked for months about the United States trying to control advanced chips and shape the rules around AI. This is the next stage of that strategy. ExportAI turns some of that talk into industrial policy. It says the U.S. government is willing to use financing tools to help trusted American systems land overseas faster. That matters for software firms, chipmakers, cloud infrastructure, and for places like Central Ohio, where the physical footprint of the AI economy keeps showing up in data centers, power planning, and land use debates.

HOST: It also sets up the other major AI story this morning, which is Nvidia. AP reports Nvidia delivered another outsized quarter, with revenue and profit again beating expectations as demand for AI chips stayed enormous. The company also authorized an eighty billion dollar buyback, which underscored how much cash the AI buildout is still throwing off.

COHOST: But the interesting part now is that huge numbers are not enough by themselves. The market expects huge.

HOST: Exactly. That is the durability test. Nvidia is still the most important scoreboard for the AI trade, but each report now has to do more than prove demand exists. It has to prove demand can stay extraordinary long enough to justify the way the entire sector is priced. So the story this morning is not that Nvidia disappointed. It did not. The story is that AI optimism remains real, but it also keeps having to clear a higher bar every quarter.

HOST: Closer to home, one of the most visible Central Ohio accountability stories moved forward this week at Sawyer Towers. WOSU reports Columbus and Franklin County leaders used the start of the demolition of the condemned apartment towers on the Near East Side to highlight new landlord accountability laws and stronger disaster-response tools adopted after the complex's collapse into crisis. Officials are trying to make the demolition mean something broader than the end of two failed buildings.

COHOST: In other words, they are trying to turn one of the city's clearest examples of housing neglect into a policy marker.

HOST: Right. The continuity language here matters because this is not just demolition theater. The city is arguing that what happened at Sawyer Towers exposed real weaknesses in enforcement, emergency response, and tenant protection. So the next question is whether those new laws actually change behavior before the next building reaches that point. With housing pressure still high across Columbus, that is not a niche issue. It is part of the broader affordability story: if more people are stretched on rent or squeezed out of ownership, then the quality and accountability of existing housing stock matters even more.

HOST: The other Columbus story we are still following is the Columbus City Schools staffing fallout. After the board voted to cut two hundred ninety-nine positions to close the last piece of a fifty million dollar budget gap, the district is now moving from vote night into implementation. That is where families, teachers, and staff will start trying to figure out where the thinner support actually shows up.

COHOST: And this is usually where abstract savings turn into concrete friction.

HOST: Exactly. The district says many of the positions were vacant and that attrition softened the immediate blow, but families are not going to judge this by spreadsheet language. They are going to judge it by whether building coverage feels weaker, whether student support is harder to access, whether transportation or maintenance gets slower, and whether next year's school-level staffing plans feel stable. So the reason this stays active is simple: the vote is over, but the consequences are just becoming visible.

HOST: At the state level, the Ohio Supreme Court has now put fresh attention on the long-running fight over pandemic unemployment benefits. The court said unemployment benefits were one of the major issues highlighted in this week's oral arguments, keeping alive the dispute over whether Governor Mike DeWine had the authority to end the federal three-hundred-dollar weekly supplement early in 2021.

COHOST: This is one of those stories where the calendar can fool you. It sounds old until you remember the money and precedent are still very live.

HOST: Exactly. The case still matters because it sits at the intersection of executive power, emergency authority, and roughly nine hundred million dollars that plaintiffs say Ohio workers were wrongly denied. Even if no ruling is immediate, the fact that the argument is getting this level of attention tells you the question is still unresolved in a meaningful way. It is also the kind of case that can quickly re-enter the political conversation if the justices signal the dispute is not moot after all.

HOST: On home lending and housing, the big national-local pattern remains the same, and it is still frustrating. Freddie Mac's latest weekly survey showed the average thirty-year fixed mortgage rate at six point three six percent as of May 14th. That is slightly lower than the prior week, but not enough to change the affordability math for most buyers. And here in Central Ohio, WOSU reported April closed sales fell thirteen point six percent from a year earlier even as inventory improved and the median sales price rose to three hundred forty-six thousand five hundred dollars.

COHOST: More choices, same payment problem.

HOST: That is the cleanest way to say it. Inventory is improving. The market is less frantic than it was in the peak frenzy years. But buyers are still running into financing that keeps the monthly payment feeling too expensive relative to incomes. So the watch item for the next few days is whether rates get any real relief from calmer energy prices and steadier bond yields. If they do not, Central Ohio may keep seeing better browsing conditions without a proportionate pickup in closings.

HOST: The markets snapshot heading into the holiday weekend captured that same split between resilience and unease. AP reports Wall Street closed out an eighth straight winning week on Friday, with the S and P 500 rising twenty-seven point seven five points to seven thousand four hundred seventy-three point four seven. The Dow gained two hundred ninety-four point zero four to fifty thousand five hundred seventy-nine point seven zero. The Nasdaq added fifty point eight seven to twenty-six thousand three hundred forty-three point nine seven.

COHOST: Stocks keep acting stronger than consumers feel.

HOST: They do. AP noted that the market stayed near records even as a consumer survey showed household sentiment falling to a record low on inflation worries tied to the Iran war. That is an important split to keep in mind. Wall Street is still being supported by solid earnings, especially in big technology and consumer names. Main Street is more focused on gas, prices, and uncertainty. If oil stays calmer, markets may keep the upper hand. If energy swings higher again, that mood gap could get a lot harder to sustain.

HOST: For Columbus weather, today is not the clean outdoor window that Friday might have looked like earlier in the week. The National Weather Service forecast updated Friday afternoon calls for showers and possible thunderstorms today, with a high near the mid-seventies and a strong chance of rain before conditions improve later Saturday night. Sunday looks better, with cooler and drier air starting to work in.

COHOST: So this is more of a radar day than a picnic day, at least for the first half.

HOST: Exactly. If you have travel, graduation plans, or backyard events, build in some flexibility today. The better part of the weekend appears to be the back half, not the front half.

HOST: The through line this morning is that pressure is not the same thing as resolution. Senate Republicans did not solve their immigration fight. They postponed it after revealing real limits on Trump's sway inside the chamber. House leaders did not settle the Iran war powers question. They delayed a vote they looked at risk of losing. Washington is actively trying to export more American AI, which shows the technology race is becoming more state-directed. Nvidia keeps proving the AI boom is still powerful, but every quarter now has to defend bigger expectations than the one before. Columbus is trying to make the Sawyer Towers failure mean stronger housing accountability, while Columbus City Schools is moving from budget decision to lived consequences. Ohio's pandemic-benefits case is still alive because emergency-era decisions do not stop mattering just because time has passed. And the housing market continues to offer more inventory without enough rate relief to make that improvement feel decisive.

COHOST: So the Saturday watch list is straightforward. Watch whether the Senate comes back from recess ready to strip out the baggage and move its immigration bill. Watch whether Iran war politics get harder for House leaders to contain. Watch whether ExportAI becomes a real pipeline or just a headline. Watch how quickly Columbus turns accountability language into visible follow-through on housing and school operations. And watch rates, because for a lot of households around here, that is still the number doing the most practical damage.

HOST: That is your Morning Brief for Saturday, May 23rd. Have a good day, stay weather-aware, and pay attention to the stories that look delayed, because several of them are really just loading up the next round.

item.description: Senate Republicans leave town after an internal revolt derails their immigration enforcement funding bill, House leaders delay an Iran war powers vote they looked set to lose, the White House pushes a new export-financing plan to spread American AI tools abroad, Nvidia clears earnings but still faces a tougher market test, Columbus City Schools moves into the service-impact phase after cutting 299 positions, the Ohio Supreme Court weighs whether Governor Mike DeWine could end federal pandemic jo
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Friday, May 22nd, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

COHOST: This morning has a real pre-holiday split-screen feel. Washington is leaving several important fights unresolved, markets are trying to decide whether lower oil is enough to calm things down, and here in Ohio the local pressure points are getting more practical, not less.

HOST: We start in Washington, where the clearest fresh development is not a bill passing, but a priority collapsing. Reuters reports Senate Republicans abandoned plans to vote on a seventy-two billion dollar immigration enforcement bill before recess after an internal revolt over two Trump-backed add-ons: a one point eight billion dollar fund for people the administration says were victims of government weaponization, and another one billion dollars for a White House ballroom.

HOST: That matters because yesterday this still looked like a question of trimming a problematic provision and salvaging the core border money. This morning the story is bigger than that. The whole vote is slipping to June. Senate Majority Leader John Thune is now openly admitting the package became more complicated than it was supposed to be, which is a polite Washington way of saying leadership lost control of a bill it had tried to frame as simple and urgent.

COHOST: And that turns this from a messaging problem into a functional one. If Republicans cannot move the cleanest version of an immigration funding package before a recess, it tells you the party's governing margin is thinner than the branding suggests.

HOST: Exactly. The continuity from yesterday still matters, but the story advanced. This is no longer just Republican discomfort with a ballroom line item. It is now a broader sign of GOP infighting, Trump fatigue inside his own conference, and real questions about whether the president's personal political demands are making it harder for his party to execute one of its core policy priorities.

HOST: The second national story is another congressional delay, but on a much more serious question. Associated Press reports House Republican leaders called off a vote on legislation that would compel President Trump to withdraw from the war with Iran after it became clear they might not have the numbers to defeat it. That pushes the issue into June and adds to the evidence that support for the war is getting less automatic on Capitol Hill.

COHOST: That is a notable shift. Earlier in this conflict, the story was whether congressional resistance would amount to anything. Now the story is that leaders are actively managing around the risk of losing.

HOST: Right. This matters in two ways. First, politically, it shows more Republicans are at least willing to make leadership sweat over a war the president began without congressional approval. Second, economically, every sign of continued instability around Iran still feeds directly into the things households actually notice: gasoline, shipping, inflation pressure, and bond yields.

HOST: If you are looking for the immediate watch item heading into the holiday weekend, it is not whether Congress ends the war today. It will not. It is whether more lawmakers decide the White House has not given them a convincing enough endgame, and whether that rising discomfort keeps energy markets on edge even during moments of temporary calm.

HOST: The biggest technology policy move in the last twenty-four hours comes from the Trump administration's attempt to export more of the American AI stack abroad. Reuters reports the White House is launching a program through the U.S. Export-Import Bank to provide billions in financing to foreign buyers of American AI tools. The idea is straightforward: make it easier for other countries and companies to buy U.S. systems, while requiring Commerce Department sign-off for sensitive technologies like advanced chips.

COHOST: So this is both industrial policy and strategic competition. Washington is not just trying to control who gets the best chips. It is also trying to subsidize the spread of the American version of AI before China can fill that gap.

HOST: That is the key point. The fresh angle is not another warning about AI risk or another theoretical executive order. It is a concrete export and financing push. In plain English, the administration wants U.S. firms to sell more AI capacity abroad, but on terms Washington can still supervise. That has implications for Nvidia, for cloud companies, for allies deciding whose infrastructure to buy, and for places like Central Ohio that keep absorbing more of the physical footprint of the AI economy through data centers and utility demand.

HOST: Which takes us directly to Nvidia, because the market is still using that company as a live referendum on how durable the AI boom really is. Reuters reported Nvidia again beat expectations, forecast second-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates, and announced an eighty billion dollar buyback. But the market reaction stayed restrained enough to send the same message we talked about yesterday, only louder today: the company can still deliver huge numbers and investors will still ask whether the numbers are huge enough.

COHOST: That is what happens when one company stops being judged like a normal stock and starts being judged like the scoreboard for an entire theme.

HOST: Exactly. Nvidia is no longer just reporting earnings. It is testing whether the market still believes AI spending can outrun valuation pressure, higher yields, and geopolitical noise. The answer this morning looks like a cautious yes, but not an easy yes. The stock story is still strong. The confidence story is a little more fragile.

HOST: Closer to home, the most important Columbus story still moving through the system remains the Columbus City Schools budget fallout. WOSU reported this week that the board voted to cut two hundred ninety-nine positions to close the final part of a fifty million dollar gap, with one hundred twelve people actually losing jobs and one hundred four of those being building substitutes.

COHOST: And this is where the conversation gets more concrete for families. The vote happened. Now the only question that matters is where the thinner staffing shows up first.

HOST: Right. District leaders say many of the eliminated roles were vacant and that attrition softened the blow, but that does not erase the practical concern. Building substitutes, counselors, custodial support, mechanics, and other day-to-day staffing roles are the connective tissue of a school system. Families may not think about those jobs every morning, but they definitely notice when coverage gets worse, response times slip, or support services become less reliable.

HOST: One reason this stays on the active list is timing. Schools are now moving from the budget decision into summer planning, staffing assignments, and fall readiness. So the next several days are likely to bring more detail about where the district thinks it can absorb the cuts and where it cannot. That is the real continuity language this morning: the budget vote is over, but the consequences are just starting to become legible.

HOST: A second Ohio story moved onto the watch list yesterday evening. The Statehouse News Bureau reports the Ohio Supreme Court will decide whether Governor Mike DeWine had the authority to end the federal three-hundred-dollar-a-week pandemic unemployment supplement early in 2021. Roughly three hundred thousand Ohioans are seeking what they say is about nine hundred million dollars in unpaid benefits.

COHOST: This is one of those stories that sounds old until you realize the legal and political stakes are very current. It is really a fight over executive authority, state obligations, and whether money that people were promised can still be reached years later.

HOST: Exactly. The state argues the case is moot because the federal program ended long ago. The plaintiffs argue DeWine lacked authority to leave the program early and that the money remained available. Even if the court takes time to rule, the fact that the case is back at the center of Ohio's legal conversation gives it immediate relevance. It is a reminder that pandemic-era decisions are still working their way through the system, especially when they involved cash, state power, and labor-market politics.

HOST: On housing and home lending, the broad message is still that better inventory has not yet translated into easier monthly payments. Reuters reported pending home sales rose for a third straight month in April, but economists still expect demand to remain subdued because borrowing costs are high, household budgets are strained, and entry-level supply remains tight. Freddie Mac's latest published weekly survey had the average thirty-year fixed mortgage at six point three six percent as of May 14th.

COHOST: And Central Ohio is basically living that exact national pattern in local form.

HOST: It is. WOSU reported Central Ohio April closed sales fell thirteen point six percent from a year earlier to two thousand two hundred two, while inventory rose and the median sales price climbed to three hundred forty-six thousand five hundred dollars. So yes, buyers have more options than they did in the frenzy years. But the extra choice is being offset by financing that still makes the payment math tough. That is why the cleanest phrase for this market remains frustrated demand, not dead demand.

HOST: If rates were meaningfully lower, this much inventory improvement would feel like relief. With rates still above six percent, it mostly feels like more listings to look at before deciding the payment is still too high.

HOST: The markets snapshot reflects that same push and pull between relief and caution. According to the Associated Press, the S and P 500 rose twelve point seven five points Thursday to seven thousand four hundred forty-five point seven two. The Dow added two hundred seventy-six point three one to fifty thousand two hundred eighty-five point sixty-six. The Nasdaq rose twenty-two point seven four to twenty-six thousand two hundred ninety-three point one zero.

COHOST: That was not a euphoric rally. It was more like a market exhale.

HOST: Exactly. AP said stocks strengthened as oil backed off sharply from the morning highs, with Brent falling from around one hundred nine dollars to settle below one hundred three. That mattered because lower oil helped ease yields as well. So the market tone heading into Friday is better than it looked earlier in the week, but it still depends on a fragile chain of assumptions: that Iran risk does not flare again, that yields do not restart their climb, and that the AI trade keeps producing enough evidence to justify the optimism priced into major tech names.

HOST: For Columbus weather, today's setup is much friendlier than the stormier tone we saw earlier this week. The National Weather Service forecast calls for mostly sunny skies and a high near eighty-one today, with a light west wind by afternoon. Tonight looks mostly clear with a low around fifty-eight.

COHOST: So today is the outdoor window.

HOST: It is. The bigger planning note is what comes next. Friday itself stays mostly fine for most of the day, but shower and thunderstorm chances start to rebuild later Friday and become more meaningful Friday night into Saturday. So if you are trying to fit in yard work, graduation travel, or any pre-holiday errands that are better done dry, today is the cleaner opportunity.

HOST: The through line this morning is unresolved pressure. Senate Republicans did not settle their immigration fight; they postponed it. House leaders did not defeat the Iran war powers challenge; they delayed that too. The White House is trying to scale American AI abroad with financing, which tells you the technology race is getting more state-directed, not less. Nvidia keeps proving the AI boom is real, but not that expectations are reasonable. Columbus City Schools finished the vote, but not the fallout. Ohio's pandemic-benefits lawsuit is back because old emergency decisions still carry live political and financial consequences. And the housing market has more homes to browse, but not yet the rate relief that would make those homes feel truly attainable.

COHOST: So the watch list for Friday is pretty clean. Watch whether Washington's delays start to look tactical or structural. Watch whether oil stays down enough to keep pressure off yields. Watch whether the AI story broadens from one great earnings report into a more convincing policy and infrastructure story. And locally, watch for the first really concrete signs of how budget cuts and high borrowing costs are shaping everyday decisions in Central Ohio.

HOST: That is your Morning Brief for Friday, May 22nd. Have a good day, and keep an eye on the stories that look paused, because a lot of them are not resolved at all. They are just moving into the next round.

Good morning. It is Thursday, May 21st, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

COHOST: Today feels less like one giant headline and more like a series of stress tests. Congress, the White House, the AI trade, school systems, and homebuyers are all getting asked whether the story underneath the headline is actually holding up.

HOST: We start in Washington, where one of the clearest signs of political strain this morning is not what Senate Republicans added to their immigration package, but what they now look ready to remove. Associated Press reports Republican leaders are expected to abandon a proposal for one billion dollars in security funding for the White House complex and President Trump's planned ballroom after pushback from their own members over timing, detail, and cost.

HOST: That matters because it tells you this bill is still unstable even before final text is out. The larger package is supposed to restore funding for ICE and the Border Patrol, and leadership still wants it passed before the Memorial Day recess. But when a White House-backed provision becomes a liability inside the president's own party, that is a sign the coalition is thinner than it looks from the outside.

COHOST: So this is not just about a ballroom. It is about whether Republicans can keep the core immigration bill from turning into a broader display of vote-count weakness.

HOST: Exactly. The fresh angle this morning is that the trimming is happening under pressure, not from Democrats, but from Republicans who do not want to defend that add-on while the party is also trying to sell border enforcement as the urgent priority. Watch whether leaders can narrow the bill cleanly, or whether more provisions get stripped and expose deeper disagreement before the week ends.

HOST: The second national story is also in Congress, but this one is about war powers. The House is expected to vote today on legislation that would compel Trump to withdraw from the war with Iran. That follows a Senate vote this week in which a small but meaningful number of Republicans crossed over to advance a similar resolution.

COHOST: That does not mean Trump is suddenly boxed in. But it does mean the argument has shifted from whether Congress will object at all to whether Republican discomfort is finally becoming visible enough to matter.

HOST: Right. The practical question here is not whether this House vote ends the conflict. It probably does not. The practical question is whether lawmakers are becoming less willing to let the White House describe the Iran war as basically managed while U.S. operations, oil risk, and legal questions are all still live. That is why this story remains important even on a morning without a major new battlefield turn. The pressure is now as much constitutional and political as it is military.

HOST: If you are looking for the immediate economic reason to keep watching Iran, it is still energy, yields, and inflation expectations. Markets got a break yesterday as oil prices fell and Treasury yields eased, but none of that becomes durable if Washington and Tehran slide back toward a sharper escalation cycle. So for today, the real watch item is whether the congressional challenge grows, and whether the White House changes its tone in response.

HOST: The biggest technology and markets story this morning is Nvidia, which once again delivered results strong enough to beat expectations and still somehow left investors asking for more. Reuters reports Nvidia forecast second-quarter revenue of about ninety-one billion dollars, above estimates, and announced an eighty billion dollar share buyback. But shares still slipped in extended trading.

COHOST: Which is a useful reminder that this market is no longer asking whether Nvidia is good. It is asking whether even exceptional numbers are enough at this valuation, in this rate environment, with this much dependence on continued AI buildout.

HOST: That is the key point. Nvidia is still functioning as a proxy for the whole AI capital spending story. If its guidance had missed, that would have looked like a direct threat to the trade. But the more subtle message from the overnight reaction is that investors now need proof not just of growth, but of durability. They want to know that the spending wave survives into 2027 and 2028, not just the next quarter.

HOST: And that leads directly into the separate AI policy story that could matter a lot for companies, infrastructure builders, and regions like Central Ohio. Reuters reports the White House's Office of the National Cyber Director briefed leading AI firms on a planned executive order that could let intelligence and other government agencies review advanced models before release. According to that report, developers could be asked to notify the government ahead of major launches and share advanced models up to ninety days before public release.

COHOST: The national policy debate is about safety and strategic visibility. The local version is about what happens when the federal government wants more oversight while places like Central Ohio keep absorbing more of the physical buildout.

HOST: That is why this is not some abstract Silicon Valley story. If Washington wants earlier access to frontier systems, it is signaling that advanced models are being treated more like critical infrastructure and national security assets. In Central Ohio, the matching reality is the continuing demand for power, land, transmission, and water tied to data-center growth. So the continuity from yesterday still holds, but the story advanced: the executive-order discussion is no longer rumor in the abstract. The White House is actively briefing firms.

HOST: Closer to home, the biggest Columbus story still moving through the system is the Columbus City Schools budget cut package. WOSU reports the district voted unanimously to cut two hundred ninety-nine positions as the final piece of a fifty million dollar reduction for the coming school year.

COHOST: And the reason this stays active is that the vote was the decision point, not the end point.

HOST: Exactly. District leaders say many of the cuts will be absorbed through open jobs, attrition, retirements, and other staffing changes, with building substitutes and attendance specialists among the main targets. But the issue for families is now much more practical than procedural. What services get thinner? Which schools feel it first? And how much can a district say cuts are furthest from the classroom before the effects still reach the classroom anyway?

HOST: This also remains one of the clearest local examples of a broader state-level squeeze. Columbus leaders are still pointing toward inadequate state funding as part of the problem, and that means the next several days are not really about whether the district cut enough. They are about whether officials can explain, in concrete terms, what gets harder next fall because fewer people are available to do the daily support work that keeps a district functioning.

HOST: On housing, the latest data still says supply is improving faster than affordability. Columbus Realtors says Central Ohio had two thousand two hundred two closed sales in April, down thirteen point six percent from a year earlier, while inventory rose thirteen point four percent, months of supply edged up to two point zero, and the median sales price climbed to three hundred forty-six thousand five hundred dollars.

COHOST: So buyers have a little more choice, but not meaningful relief.

HOST: That is the story. At the statewide level, Ohio Realtors says April home sales fell three percent from a year ago while the median price rose seven point nine percent to two hundred sixty-nine thousand nine hundred dollars. And Reuters reports pending home sales nationally increased for a third straight month in April, but economists still expect housing demand to stay subdued because mortgage rates remain high and household budgets are still under strain.

HOST: The most recent Freddie Mac benchmark, released May 14th, had the thirty-year fixed mortgage at six point three six percent. Since then, the bigger market signal has been bond volatility. Rates may not look dramatically different week to week, but for borrowers the effect is the same: monthly payments are still high enough to cancel out a lot of the benefit from better inventory. So if you are trying to read the Central Ohio market this morning, the answer is not frozen demand. It is frustrated demand.

HOST: The markets snapshot reflects that balance between relief and fragility. AP reports the S and P 500 rose seventy-nine point three six points Wednesday to seven thousand four hundred thirty-two point ninety-seven. The Dow gained six hundred forty-five point four seven to fifty thousand nine point three five. The Nasdaq added three hundred ninety-nine point six five to twenty-six thousand two hundred seventy point three six.

COHOST: That was the market taking a breath after yields cooled and oil backed off. But now the handoff is from relief rally to proof test.

HOST: Right. Reuters also reported that the ten-year Treasury yield rose again in Thursday trading after Wednesday's pause, while Nvidia's strong numbers helped lift chip sentiment globally. So the market tone this morning is better than it was earlier in the week, but not settled. Investors still need lower energy stress, less yield pressure, and enough AI earnings strength to keep risk appetite from rolling back over.

HOST: For Columbus weather, the National Weather Service digital forecast shows a much calmer day than yesterday. After the rain and storm chances moved through, today looks dry with temperatures climbing gradually from the upper forties and low fifties this morning into the low seventies this afternoon. Winds stay out of the northeast, and rain chances remain near zero through the day.

COHOST: Translation: this is the reset day. Cooler air, better windows outside, and a break before the next round of unsettled weather lines up for Friday.

HOST: Exactly. Friday's forecast starts loading rain chances back in, especially later in the day, so today is the cleaner outdoor day if you need one. Commutes should be easier, the air will feel a lot less heavy, and the bigger planning note is simply not to confuse today's calm with a stable stretch heading into the weekend.

HOST: The through line this morning is that a lot of important systems are still functioning, but under visible strain. Senate Republicans are finding out that even a friendly majority does not eliminate political limits. Congress is still testing how much war authority it is willing to hand the White House on Iran. Nvidia is discovering that dominance does not automatically satisfy a market that now expects perfection. The White House wants more visibility into advanced AI models just as communities like Central Ohio keep inheriting more of the hardware footprint. Columbus City Schools made the vote, but still has to prove the cuts do not erode daily support where families feel it most. And homebuyers have more listings, but not yet the financing relief that would make those options truly usable.

COHOST: Taipei is not being subtle here. It is trying to drag the conversation back from transaction to deterrence.

So this story remains active because the White House still has not offered the kind of plain, unmistakable clarification that markets, allies, and Beijing would all understand the same way. COHOST: So the fresh angle is not just procedure. It is coalition strain.

If more pieces get challenged or stripped, the broader takeaway will be that the party's procedural lane is narrower than its message discipline suggests.

Now it is cutting nearly 300 more positions to finish the budget math. So the watch is what this means operationally once summer planning turns into the actual school year. Do attendance problems worsen? Does building coverage get thinner? Does the state funding argument create any immediate pressure in Columbus or at the Statehouse? It does not magically solve payment shock when mortgage rates are still in the mid-sixes and household budgets are getting squeezed by food, insurance, and energy costs. So the fresh takeaway this morning is that the buyer bottleneck remains cost, not demand. People still want homes. The monthly payment still keeps too many of them from acting comfortably.

In plain English, the administration appears to be moving from broad talk about AI safety toward a more formal pre-release review structure for frontier systems with serious cyber capabilities.

But it also underscores a tension this region keeps living with: the country wants more AI capacity, and places like Central Ohio are expected to host more of the infrastructure without having all the political leverage over the rules or the downstream costs. That is why this remains a live story rather than a niche tech story.

The newest turn is from Taipei, where Reuters reported overnight that Taiwan is now openly welcoming a direct call between President Trump and President Lai Ching-te as officials there try to calm the fallout from Trump's comments after the Beijing meeting.

That response matters because it confirms what we have been tracking since the summit closed. Taiwan heard Trump's remarks the same way markets, allies, and strategic planners heard them: as a signal that U.S. arms support may now be treated less like a standing deterrent and more like a negotiating variable. The Associated Press reported Sunday that Lai stressed U.S. arms purchases remain the most important deterrent to regional conflict and instability. In other words, Taiwan is trying to pull the conversation back to first principles before uncertainty hardens into a new policy baseline.

So the continuity line is sharper this morning. This is no longer just about diplomatic tone after a high-profile summit. It is about whether the United States is blurring a long-standing line around deterrence at the exact moment China wants more room to test that line. If Washington clarifies quickly, the damage may stay rhetorical. If it does not, then every market already sensitive to oil, shipping, semiconductors, and defense risk has another reason to stay nervous.

Why should listeners in Ohio care? Because Taiwan risk is not a remote abstraction. It runs through chip supply, manufacturing confidence, shipping insurance, energy pricing, and capital spending. If the post-summit message remains muddy, it becomes one more source of inflation pressure and one more excuse for markets to price in a harder path on rates.

The second national story is still in the Senate, where Republicans are trying to keep a broad immigration enforcement package alive while the parliamentarian keeps forcing rewrites. The Associated Press reported late Saturday that a proposal to include one billion dollars for White House security additions tied to the president's ballroom project failed Senate procedural rules and cannot stay in the package as drafted.

That does not end the bill, but it reinforces the same problem we talked about over the weekend. The narrower the reconciliation lane becomes, the harder it is to carry extra priorities inside it. Senate Republicans are still trying to move roughly seventy two billion dollars in immigration-related funding through a process that leaves very little room for anything that looks too broad, too incidental, or too loosely tied to budget rules.

The practical consequence is bigger than one rejected line item. Every forced revision eats time, narrows options, and exposes internal fault lines about what the party actually views as essential. If leadership keeps having to redraft, refine, and resubmit, then the story stops being just whether Republicans support tougher enforcement. It becomes whether they can write a bill disciplined enough to survive their own chosen procedure.

That makes this a real proof-phase week. Watch whether the Senate stabilizes the core of the package, or whether more provisions get stripped and the coalition begins to look thinner than advertised.

The third national story this morning is not a brand-new headline, but it is still an active piece of the wider political map. The Supreme Court's decision late last week preserved access to mifepristone while the legal fight continues, so the immediate disruption to patients and providers has been avoided for now. The practical reality remains that women can still get the medication by mail and through pharmacies without a required in-person doctor visit while the appeal moves forward.

The reason it still belongs in the brief is that the calm is operational, not final. The underlying fight over how far courts can reach into long-settled FDA decisions is still alive, and it remains one of the clearest examples of how legal risk can keep hanging over national policy even after an immediate cliff has been moved back. The short-term situation stabilized. The long-term precedent is still unresolved.

Back here in Columbus, the biggest local story remains Issue 5, but the framing changes a little on a Monday because this is no longer a campaign story at all. Columbus City Council is back in session today, and the city enters another civic work week with voters having already delivered a clear verdict. The question now is not whether the charter amendment had support. The question is whether the city can show actual implementation structure for the expanded community crisis response system.

That means the same operational questions still define the story. Who owns execution inside city government? What milestones will be public? How will dispatch rules change? Which calls move away from a police-first posture? What hiring timeline exists? What clinical and nonprofit partnerships are actually being built? And when should residents expect to see something more concrete than general language about commitment and progress?

The reason to keep this story hot is simple. A seventy-seven percent vote share settles legitimacy, but it does not settle administration. Columbus now owes residents a visible implementation path, and every meeting week that begins without that path becoming clearer raises the odds that the city drifts from mandate into muddle.

The second local story is still the full housing ladder problem in Central Ohio. WOSU's latest housing reporting showed April closed sales down 13.6 percent from a year ago to 2,202, even as inventory improved. That might sound like some market cooling, but the median price still hit 346,500 dollars. So the region may be getting a little more selection, but affordability has not meaningfully broken in favor of buyers.

And that is only the upper-middle rung of the ladder. On the harder edge of the same problem, WOSU's homelessness reporting this month showed 2,587 people experiencing homelessness in Columbus and Franklin County, with a notable rise in people living outside even as shelter use fell. Community Shelter Board leaders said they want to acquire three hotels to relieve pressure, and city officials have already acknowledged that the added 7.2 million dollars in the budget is not enough by itself.

That is why the continuity line still matters. Central Ohio is not just experiencing a housing market that feels expensive. It is experiencing a system where pressure is visible at every level at once. Buyers face high prices and high borrowing costs. Renters face scarce affordable units. Service systems face stronger shelter strain. And the unsheltered count says some people are simply being pushed all the way out of the formal market.

So the next five-day watch is not abstract. Do local officials connect the positive-sounding inventory story to any visible action on affordability, shelter capacity, hotel acquisition, or the bond-funded housing pipeline? If not, then the region is still mostly describing the pressure rather than relieving it.

On home lending and mortgages, the official weekly benchmark remains Freddie Mac's May 14 survey, which showed the average 30-year fixed rate at 6.36 percent, barely down from 6.37 percent the prior week. Technically that is an improvement. In real household terms, it is still a heavy financing environment.

More importantly, the daily market has been less friendly than the weekly average suggests. Mortgage News Daily's rate index ended Friday at 6.65 percent for a top-tier 30-year fixed loan, up sharply as bond yields climbed. That difference is worth explaining because it tells the real story. Freddie Mac gives the slower-moving weekly average based on completed application data. Mortgage News Daily gives a more immediate view of lender pricing as rate markets swing. Put them together, and the message is consistent: the mortgage market is not improving in a durable way yet. It is wobbling around an elevated baseline.

For Central Ohio, that matters because even a modest local increase in inventory does not help much if financing costs keep offsetting it. More people can look. Fewer can comfortably act. That is why affordability still feels frozen even when some of the headline supply numbers appear to be softening in the right direction.

The AI and technology story this morning is a useful reminder that Washington is still arguing with itself about whether advanced models should mainly be accelerated, tested, restricted, or all three. Axios reported overnight that more than sixty Trump allies, including Steve Bannon and other prominent MAGA figures, are pressing the White House to test and approve the most powerful AI models before they are broadly released.

That is politically notable because it widens the pressure beyond the bipartisan lawmaker concerns we were already watching last week. This new letter suggests part of Trump's own coalition is also moving toward the view that the government cannot stay mostly hands-off once models become powerful enough to discover vulnerabilities at scale or automate more offensive cyber work.

Good morning. It is Sunday, May 17th, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

We begin this morning with the story that still sits above almost everything else because it now touches diplomacy, energy, markets, and military risk all at once. The Trump-Xi summit is over, but the real takeaway from the last twenty four hours is not that tensions disappeared. It is that one of the biggest unresolved points just got more explicit.

The Associated Press reported Saturday that President Trump, speaking after his trip to Beijing, described arms sales to Taiwan as a very good negotiating chip in dealings with China. That is a blunt phrase, and it matters because it sharpens the continuity line we have been tracking since the summit began. The issue is not whether Washington and Beijing can stage a calmer tone for a few days. The issue is whether core strategic commitments are becoming bargaining material.

Taiwan has always been the live wire in this relationship, and China made that clear again during the summit. What changed over the last day is that Trump publicly suggested the delayed arms package could remain in abeyance depending on China. That leaves allies, markets, and military planners with the same immediate question: is this temporary negotiation language, or is it a sign that deterrence itself is being repriced?

Why does that matter to listeners far from Washington and Beijing? Because unresolved Taiwan risk does not stay neatly inside foreign policy. It runs straight into shipping routes, semiconductor supply chains, energy nerves, defense spending, and investor confidence. If that uncertainty grows, then oil stays sensitive, inflation stays harder to cool, and borrowing costs stay heavier than households want them to be.

So this is still the same summit aftermath story, but the framing is more serious this morning. Last week we were asking whether the visit would produce proof instead of theater. Today the proof test is even simpler. Do tensions actually cool, or did the trip just make clearer which pressure points remain available for leverage.

The second national story is still on the Senate side, where the immigration enforcement package we have been following is now looking even more procedurally fragile. The Associated Press reported late Saturday that the Senate parliamentarian ruled against a proposal to include one billion dollars for White House security additions and the president's ballroom project inside the broader Republican bill for immigration enforcement agencies.

That ruling does not kill the whole package, but it adds to the larger pattern that was already visible on Friday. Republicans are trying to move a roughly seventy two billion dollar bill through a narrow reconciliation path, and the parliamentarian keeps reminding them that the path is in fact narrow. Every provision that gets knocked out or rewritten increases the time pressure, the drafting pressure, and the political pressure.

This is why the continuity line on that story remains important. The bill is no longer just a message vehicle about border toughness. It is becoming a test of whether Senate Republicans can separate what is core from what is ornamental, keep the coalition together, and survive the procedural gauntlet without losing momentum before committee work and floor planning get tighter.

The practical thing to watch over the next several days is not only whether they can rewrite the rejected pieces. It is whether the repeated rulings expose a deeper problem inside the package itself. If leadership has to keep trimming and restructuring, then disagreements about cost, scope, and side priorities become much harder to hide.

National story number three is a legal and institutional fight that remains highly relevant even without a fresh overnight turn. The Supreme Court's decision on Thursday preserved broad access to mifepristone while the lawsuit continues, which means the practical situation for patients and providers is stable this weekend. Women can still get the medication through pharmacies or the mail without an in person doctor visit while the appeal process plays out.

The reason this remains an active national story is that the immediate outcome and the larger precedent are not the same thing. The short term access question is calmer for now. The longer term question about how aggressively courts can second guess the Food and Drug Administration after years of regulation is still unresolved. So the right read this morning is that disruption was delayed, not that the institutional fight is over.

Back here in Columbus, the local continuity story still starts with Issue 5 because the campaign phase is finished and the execution phase is now the only thing that matters. Voters approved the expansion of a community crisis response system. The mandate is real. The question now is whether City Hall will convert that mandate into public structure fast enough for residents to see what actually changes.

That means implementation questions are no longer side details. They are the story. Who is in charge. What milestones are public. How does dispatch change. Which calls move out of a police-first posture. What staffing model gets used. Which clinical or nonprofit partners are brought in. And what timeline is realistic for visible operations rather than talking points.

Nothing in the last day suggests those questions have been answered at the level the public should expect. So this remains one of the most important Columbus stories to keep alive through the coming week. Big election margins settle legitimacy. They do not settle execution.

The second major Central Ohio story is still housing pressure, and the latest local numbers keep supporting the same conclusion. WOSU reported on May 14 that April home sales in Central Ohio fell 13.6 percent from a year earlier to 2,202 closed sales, even as inventory improved. That sounds at first like a softer market, but the median price still reached 346,500 dollars. So yes, supply is improving at the margin. No, affordability is not suddenly fixed.

That local housing picture still connects directly to the harder edge of the story, which is homelessness and shelter strain. WOSU's May 6 reporting on the annual count found 2,587 people experiencing homelessness in Columbus and Franklin County, with the number of people living outside rising sharply while shelter use declined. That is the warning sign to keep in view. This is not only a frustrating ownership market. It is a region where more vulnerable residents are being pushed further outside the formal housing system.

That is why the continuity line still holds this morning. Central Ohio is not dealing with one housing problem. It is dealing with a full ladder problem. Buyers feel it through prices and financing. Renters feel it through scarcity and cost burden. Service systems feel it through shelter compression and rising unsheltered counts. Over the next five days, the watch item is whether any local official pairs optimistic language about inventory with something concrete on affordability, shelter capacity, or bond-backed housing delivery.

On home lending and mortgages, the official benchmark still says the average thirty year fixed rate eased to 6.36 percent in Freddie Mac's May 14 survey, down a hair from 6.37 percent the week before. That is technically good news. It is also not enough to change behavior in any meaningful way. Mid-six percent mortgages are still a payment problem, especially in a region where home prices have stayed stubborn.

And there is a second layer that matters this morning. Mortgage News Daily's index showed a sharper move higher by Friday, with the top tier thirty year fixed rate at 6.65 percent after a volatile week in the bond market. The reason to mention both numbers is that they are measuring different things, but together they tell an honest story. The official weekly benchmark says mortgage costs are still elevated. The daily market is warning that rate relief remains fragile if Treasury yields and oil keep rising.

So for buyers, refinancers, and anyone thinking about moving, the mortgage story this morning is not relief. It is instability around a still-heavy level. The market can function there, but households have to compromise. They buy less house, move farther out, wait longer, or negotiate harder for concessions. The underlying affordability drag is still very much with us.

In AI and technology, the most important development is that Washington still does not look aligned on how to govern the next generation of cyber-capable models, even as the warnings around those models are getting more urgent. Axios reported this week that Palo Alto Networks says frontier systems including Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI's GPT-5.5-Cyber are already finding vulnerabilities at a pace serious enough to trigger talk of a coming vulnerability surge. Axios also reported that White House action on AI testing and oversight is being slowed by internal disagreement over how aggressive that framework should be.

That split matters because the policy argument is no longer abstract. The question is not simply whether powerful models should exist. They already do. The question is who gets access first, who tests them, what standards govern deployment, and how much of the government's posture should focus on economic speed versus defensive control.

This national fight still has a direct Central Ohio angle because the physical infrastructure of the AI buildout keeps landing in places like this region. Power demand, water demand, semiconductor capacity, data center siting, transmission stress, and local political backlash are all part of the same story. We have already seen that tension in the Sunbury data center moratorium. So even when Washington's fight sounds theoretical, the local version is concrete: can Central Ohio absorb the infrastructure load that national AI ambition keeps implying.

The markets snapshot this morning is a reminder that record highs can reverse quickly when inflation pressure starts looking less hypothetical. On Friday, the Associated Press and Reuters both reported that U.S. stocks fell sharply as higher oil prices pushed bond yields up and rattled the market's AI-driven momentum trade. The Dow dropped a little over one percent. The S and P 500 fell about 1.2 percent. The Nasdaq lost roughly 1.4 to 1.5 percent, depending on the final reporting cut, and the ten year Treasury yield pushed up to around 4.58 to 4.60 percent.

It is saying the inflation cushion is thinner than investors wanted to believe. If oil remains elevated and yields stay firm, then high-valuation growth stocks become harder to price generously, and rate-sensitive sectors like housing feel the pressure almost immediately.

So the practical read for Monday's open is straightforward. Investors are still willing to believe in earnings and AI, but they are much less willing to ignore energy and rates. The next move depends on whether crude settles down and whether the bond market believes inflation risk is stabilizing rather than spreading.

For Columbus weather, forecast services are pointing to a warmer and more unsettled finish to the weekend. Ease Weather's Sunday forecast for Columbus showed a high near 28 degrees Celsius, about 82 degrees Fahrenheit, with some rain in the picture, followed by another warm day on Monday near 29 Celsius, or roughly 84 Fahrenheit. The useful takeaway is not the exact decimal. It is that we are turning warmer, a bit stickier, and not entirely dry.

So if you have outdoor plans today, expect a more summer-like feel than what we had earlier in the week, and keep some flexibility around showers. The cleaner weather window is not as obvious as it was on Saturday, and early next week looks warm enough that any added humidity will be noticeable fast.

The through line this morning is that almost every major story is now moving from headline phase into proof phase.

Trump and Xi can talk about a stable framework, but the Taiwan question just reminded everyone where the real leverage and risk still sit. Senate Republicans can promise a big immigration package, but parliamentary rulings keep forcing them to prove they can actually pass one. The Supreme Court preserved mifepristone access, but the larger contest over FDA authority is still alive. Columbus voters approved Issue 5, but approval is not implementation. Central Ohio housing may be normalizing in volume, but it is not normalizing in affordability, and homelessness data says the pressure is spreading downward. Mortgage rates can edge lower in a weekly survey, but daily lending costs can still jump the moment bond markets get nervous. Washington wants the benefits of frontier AI, but it still has not settled the rules for testing or access. And Wall Street still wants to believe in growth, but Friday was a reminder that oil and yields can interrupt that story very quickly.

So here is what to watch between now and midweek: whether Trump or the White House clarifies the status of the Taiwan arms package, whether Senate Republicans keep losing pieces of their immigration bill or finally stabilize the draft, whether any mifepristone follow-up broadens the political fight, whether Columbus officials offer even one concrete implementation milestone for Issue 5, whether local housing and homelessness leaders attach real policy action to the latest warning signs, whether mortgage volatility settles down, whether the White House narrows its AI testing approach, and whether markets can regain their footing without pretending inflation risk is gone.

That is your Morning Brief for Sunday, May 17th. Stay cool, keep an eye on the sky, and keep paying attention to the stories that now need measurable follow through instead of confident language.

A one basis point improvement does not change that. It only tells you the market has not gotten worse this week.

That is why the Columbus housing story and the mortgage story still belong in the same frame. Inventory can rise. Competition can cool from absurd to merely intense. But until borrowing costs come down in a more meaningful way, affordability stays under pressure.

In AI and technology, the policy story still looks slower and messier than the commercial story. At the most vulnerable end of the market, the safety net is absorbing more visible strain.

That is why housing remains one of the most important Columbus stories to keep on the front burner. It is not only about whether prices cool. It is about whether the region can produce enough actual relief, whether through more housing supply, better shelter capacity, stronger supportive services, or some combination that changes the math before the next winter cycle starts coming into view.

On home lending and mortgages, the national data still says buyers are trying to hang in, even though rates are not giving them much help. The Mortgage Bankers Association said this week that mortgage applications rose 1.7 percent from the prior week, with purchase applications up 4 percent and running 7 percent above the same week a year ago. But MBA also said the average contract rate for a conforming 30-year mortgage reached 6.46 percent, the highest level in five weeks.

So whether you lean on MBA's more immediate application data or Freddie Mac's weekly benchmark, the basic conclusion is unchanged this morning. Demand is proving more resilient than many expected, but the monthly-payment burden is still doing real damage.

That remains a Central Ohio story in a very practical sense. When rates hold in the mid-sixes, buyers in Columbus get pushed toward compromises. They look farther from the core. They accept smaller homes. They stretch their budgets. Or they step back and wait. WOSU's new April sales data reinforces that this spring is not collapsing, but it is also not normal. Activity is surviving rather than flowing.

In AI and technology, the policy side of the story still looks less settled than the money side. Axios reported this week that lawmakers are pressing the White House to act on AI cyber threats, even while a separate Axios report says internal infighting is slowing any broader executive action. One of the live disagreements is over where advanced model testing should sit and who should have the lead when the government decides whether powerful systems are safe enough for sensitive use.

That matters because the private market is moving much faster than the governance structure. Companies are still deploying, funding, and buying as if the buildout is unavoidable. Policymakers are still arguing over what kind of testing, contracting, and oversight should come first. So the U.S. position this morning is not anti-AI and not exactly pro-guardrail either. It is pro-speed with unresolved supervision.

That is where the national AI debate continues to intersect with Central Ohio. Our region remains tied to the physical layer of the technology race: semiconductors, data centers, power demand, water demand, and the broader question of whether local infrastructure can keep up with national ambition. Even when the headline is about Washington infighting, the local implication is still about whether Columbus and the surrounding counties can support the next round of industrial and digital buildout without creating new bottlenecks.

The Associated Press separately noted that the Dow climbed back above 50,000 while the Nasdaq set another record. Technology shares led the way again, helped by Cisco and broader chip strength.

The message from markets is pretty clear. Investors still believe earnings can absorb a lot, and they still want exposure to tech and AI. But the rally is not floating free of reality. It is still happening alongside elevated geopolitical tension, sticky inflation pressure, and borrowing costs that remain painful for households. So the market's mood this morning is confident, but not exactly relaxed.

If the Trump-Xi aftermath reduces stress around trade and Iran, the rally has room to keep breathing. If oil jumps, if yields push higher, or if Washington injects new instability into the immigration or AI stories, the market's tolerance could narrow again. So yes, records matter, but so does the quality of the foundation underneath them.

Tonight brings a chance of showers and thunderstorms after about 2 a.m., with a low around 57. Saturday stays warm, with a chance of showers and thunderstorms and a high near 85. So the practical weather note is simple. Today is the best balance point before the air turns more summerlike. The dry, comfortable stretch is limited. If you have outdoor plans late tonight or this weekend, pay attention to the storm timing because the warmer pattern is arriving with more instability.

The through-line this morning is that the biggest stories are still asking the same question in different forms: can institutions convert temporary calm into durable proof. Trump and Xi can say the right things, but only markets and supply chains can confirm whether risk is really coming down. The Supreme Court has preserved mifepristone access for now, but the wider legal challenge to federal regulatory authority is still alive. Senate Republicans have real immigration bill text, which means the coming fight is now about cost, rules, and discipline, not just messaging.

Housing data says inventory may be improving at the margin, but affordability is still biting and homelessness is still flashing red. Washington still wants the upside of AI without having fully settled the enforcement structure around its risks. And Wall Street keeps climbing, but under the same inflation and geopolitical weather we have been discussing all week.
